derivation_notes: Using I = integral(r**2*dm) with uniform areal density M/(pi*R**2) and annular mass element dm = 2*pi*r*M/(pi*R**2)*dr, integration from r = 0 to r = R gives I = M*R**2/2.

Dimensionless radial-density grading parameter in the areal-density profile rho(r) proportional to 1 + radial_grading*(r/R)**2, with negative values center-loading and positive values rim-loading.

new_symbol_range_suggestions.radial_grading: (-1, oo); practical benchmark range about [-0.9, 3] to keep areal density nonnegative on 0<=r<=R and provide observable center-heavy to rim-heavy contrast

derivation_notes: Relax uniform areal density by taking rho(r)=rho0*(1 + radial_grading*(r/R)**2), which remains nonnegative for radial_grading>-1. Enforcing the same total mass M and integrating I=integral r**2 dm over the disk gives the shape factor (3 + radial_grading)/(6), so radial grading directly changes the scored static mapping.
change_summary: The disk is no longer assumed uniformly dense; a new radial-grading input lets otherwise identical M and R disks have different inertia. Rim-heavy grading increases the prefactor above 1/2, while center-heavy grading decreases it below 1/2.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: The disk has uniform areal density across radius.
assumption_audit.mechanism: Nonuniform areal density redistributes mass toward smaller or larger radii, altering the radial weighting in the inertia integral at fixed total mass and outer radius.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: At radial_grading=0 the areal density becomes uniform and the successor reduces exactly to I=M*R**2/2.

response_change.parent_relation: With uniform areal density, rotational inertia is a separable product I=(1/2)MR**2, so at fixed M the slope dI/d(R**2)=M/2 is independent of any other condition and all disks share one mass-distribution factor.
response_change.child_relation: Release the uniform-density assumption by allowing a radially graded disk, so I remains proportional to M and R**2 but with a shape factor that varies with an independently sampled radial-grading input; the mapping becomes non-separable across M, R, and grading because the effective prefactor changes with grading.
response_change.observable_effect: At fixed M and R, disks with edge-heavy mass distribution have larger I than uniform disks, while center-heavy disks have smaller I; equivalently, the slope versus R**2 at fixed M differs across grading conditions.

evolution_contract.activation_condition: Observable when the experiment includes disks of equal total M and outer radius R but different admissible radial density profiles, with grading strong enough that mass is measurably shifted inward or outward while remaining nonnegative over 0<=r<=R.
evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: Within training, modest radial grading already changes the prefactor away from 1/2; in holdout, stronger but still physical grading extends the same monotone contrast between center-heavy and rim-heavy disks.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: As the radial density profile approaches uniform areal density, the shape factor returns to 1/2 and the parent law is recovered exactly.
evolution_contract.promotion_reason: The current inputs M and R do not identify how mass is distributed within the disk; a new independently sampled static input is needed to encode radial grading because different profiles can share the same M and R yet produce different I.
evolution_contract.domain_mechanism: radial mass redistribution in a rigid disk
evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: Nonuniform areal density redistributes mass toward the center or rim, changing the radial weighting in the inertia integral without changing total mass or outer radius.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: This is harder than a coefficient-only correction because the new input controls a competing center-loading versus rim-loading effect in the inertia integral, so one shared constant cannot fit samples that have identical M and R but different internal radial mass distributions.
evolution_contract.assumption_before: The disk is perfectly rigid and uniformly dense.
evolution_contract.assumption_after: The disk remains rigid but may have a radially graded areal density profile parameterized by radial_grading.
evolution_contract.observable_signature: Parent response relationship: with one shared uniform-density factor, I is fixed by M*R**2 alone. Child change: when radial_grading varies while total M and outer radius R are held fixed, the target mapping itself changes because the inertia prefactor shifts below 1/2 for center-heavy disks and above 1/2 for rim-heavy disks. This is observable for admissible grading with radial_grading>-1 so the areal density stays nonnegative over 0<=r<=R; under those conditions the slope of I versus R**2 at fixed M becomes M*(1/2 + radial_grading/6) instead of one universal M/2.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce this because the parent assigns exactly one inertial prefactor to all samples, so disks sharing the same M and R must share the same predicted I. Across experiments that vary radial_grading at fixed M and R, the child predicts distinct inertias from genuine mass-redistribution physics; no global retuning of the parent's lone constant can simultaneously match smaller center-heavy and larger rim-heavy values under the same M and R.

evolution_plan.activation_condition: Observable when the experiment includes disks of equal total M and outer radius R but different admissible radial density profiles, with grading strong enough that mass is measurably shifted inward or outward while remaining nonnegative over 0<=r<=R.
evolution_plan.train_hidden_contrast: Within training, modest radial grading already changes the prefactor away from 1/2; in holdout, stronger but still physical grading extends the same monotone contrast between center-heavy and rim-heavy disks.
evolution_plan.continuation_path: As the radial density profile approaches uniform areal density, the shape factor returns to 1/2 and the parent law is recovered exactly.
evolution_plan.promotion_reason: The current inputs M and R do not identify how mass is distributed within the disk; a new independently sampled static input is needed to encode radial grading because different profiles can share the same M and R yet produce different I.
evolution_plan.gap_statement: The current model assumes all disks with the same total mass and radius have identical inertia, omitting physically realistic radial density grading within the disk.
evolution_plan.baseline_assumption: The disk is perfectly rigid and uniformly dense.
evolution_plan.scientific_mechanism: Nonuniform areal density redistributes mass toward the center or rim, changing the radial weighting in the inertia integral without changing total mass or outer radius.
evolution_plan.rationale: Parent response relationship: for independently varied M and R under a single shared uniform-density assumption, I is exactly proportional to M*R**2 with one fixed shape factor 1/2. Changed target mapping: if radial grading is allowed as an experimental condition, the scored target itself changes because two disks with the same supplied M and R no longer need have the same I; the prefactor becomes grading-dependent, not merely an auxiliary unobserved trajectory. Distinguishing condition: vary radial grading across disks while holding total M and outer radius R fixed; then compare measured I. The parent predicts no contrast at all across those conditions, whereas the child predicts larger I for rim-loaded disks and smaller I for center-loaded disks. This is scientifically admissible for fabricated composite disks, disks with variable porosity, or bonded annular laminations, provided density stays nonnegative and the axis remains central and perpendicular. A single refit of the parent cannot absorb this across conditions because changing its lone constant rescales all samples equally and cannot assign different inertial prefactors to different grading conditions at the same M and R. Limitation: if all sampled disks are truly uniform, this mechanism is inactive and no increased target complexity is justified.

Axial thickness of the solid disk or cylinder in meters, treated as an independently varied geometric input.
derivation_notes: The parent law assumes a negligibly thin lamina. Releasing axial thickness as an input adds a finite-3D-shape contribution; the nested factor tanh(thickness/R) makes the correction negligible in the thin limit while activating it smoothly for moderately thick cylinders.
change_summary: Added a thickness-dependent inertia term for finite solid cylinders. This creates a new observable interaction through the aspect ratio thickness/R, so otherwise matched disks can have different inertia when thickness varies.

add_term_audit.mechanism_claim: A non-negligible axial extent changes the three-dimensional mass distribution of the rotating body, so the central-axis rotational inertia is not determined by face radius and radial grading alone.
add_term_audit.parent_reduction: As thickness/R -> 0, tanh(thickness/R) -> 0 and the added term vanishes, recovering the thin-disk parent law.
add_term_audit.observable_signature: At fixed M, R, and radial_grading, inertia acquires a systematic upward shift with increasing thickness, with little change for very thin disks and growing departure for thickness-to-radius ratios of order 0.1 or larger.

response_change.parent_relation: I is bilinear in M and R**2 with a single linear dependence on radial_grading, so the effect of radial_grading is the same at all otherwise equivalent disks once M and R are specified.
response_change.child_relation: Add a finite-thickness shape contribution so inertia depends on the interaction between radius and axial thickness: the radial_grading-controlled in-plane term remains, but an additional thickness-dependent term changes I even when M, R, and radial_grading are held comparable across thin and moderately thick disks.
response_change.observable_effect: For disks with the same M, R, and radial_grading trend but different thickness-to-radius ratio, the child predicts a systematic upward offset in I that grows with thickness, whereas the parent predicts no change because thickness is absent.

evolution_contract.activation_condition: Observable when the benchmark is extended beyond negligibly thin disks to finite-thickness solid cylinders with thickness not asymptotically small compared with R; practically, thickness-to-radius ratios of order 0.1 or larger produce a measurable departure from the thin-disk law.
evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: Within training on mostly thin disks the parent appears adequate, but in holdout including moderately thick specimens the same mass-radius-grading trend acquires a thickness-dependent upward shift that the parent cannot express.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: Recover the parent in the thin-limit as thickness-to-radius tends to zero, where the finite-thickness correction vanishes and the areal-density-based disk law is restored.
evolution_contract.promotion_reason: Thickness is not inferable from M, R, and radial_grading alone because disks with the same total mass and face-density grading can have different axial extent; a new sampled geometric input is required to expose finite-thickness effects.
evolution_contract.domain_mechanism: finite axial thickness contribution to rotational inertia
evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: Finite axial thickness changes the three-dimensional mass distribution of a rotating solid cylinder, adding a thickness-dependent contribution to the central-axis rotational inertia beyond the thin-face approximation.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: The added term is not a simple linear thickness offset; it combines declared quantities into the aspect ratio thickness/R and then applies a nonlinear map tanh(...), so activation depends on geometry rather than a coefficient-only rescaling.
evolution_contract.assumption_before: Disk thickness is negligible relative to its radius.
evolution_contract.assumption_after: The body can be a finite-thickness solid cylinder whose aspect ratio modulates an added inertia contribution.
evolution_contract.observable_signature: At fixed M, R, and radial_grading, disks of larger thickness show a systematic upward shift in I that grows with thickness-to-radius ratio, unlike the parent which predicts no thickness dependence.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce this because the parent expression has no thickness coordinate at all, so any two samples with identical M, R, and radial_grading must receive identical predictions. Retuning the existing coefficients cannot generate a thickness-conditioned separation across mixed-thickness specimens without changing all matched thin-disk predictions as well.

evolution_plan.gap_statement: The current law treats the object as a negligibly thin lamina, omitting the real geometric contribution from finite axial thickness in a solid disk/cylinder.

evolution_plan.scientific_mechanism: Finite axial thickness changes the three-dimensional mass distribution of a rotating solid cylinder, adding a thickness-dependent contribution to the central-axis rotational inertia beyond the thin-face approximation.
evolution_plan.rationale: Parent response relationship: at fixed M and R, inertia changes linearly with radial_grading with slope M*R**2/6, and at fixed M and radial_grading it scales only with R**2. The scientific gap is the thin-disk assumption. A realistic successor is to release finite thickness as an independent geometric input and add the corresponding 3D shape contribution. Distinguishing condition: vary thickness across otherwise similar solid disks while holding M, R, and radial_grading fixed or matched; the parent predicts identical I because thickness is absent, while the child predicts larger I for thicker specimens. This is a changed target mapping, not merely an auxiliary trajectory change, because the scored static relation itself gains dependence on the new input. The effect is admissible only when specimens are not effectively laminar; if thickness is truly negligible throughout the dataset, the refinement would be unobservable. A single refit of the parent's existing parameters cannot absorb this across mixed thickness conditions because the parent has no thickness coordinate and therefore must assign the same I to all samples with identical M, R, and radial_grading, whereas the child separates them by geometry.
